RoboTwin 2.0: A Scalable Data Generator and Benchmark with Strong Domain Randomization for Robust Bimanual Robotic Manipulation

An MLLM-driven, self-repairing code-generation pipeline pairs with five axes of scene-level domain randomization to turn a 731-object asset library into a 50-task, five-embodiment benchmark — and the paper's own tables show it's the randomization, not just more synthetic data, that buys sim-to-real robustness.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Simulation-based data synthesis is the practical alternative to collecting real bimanual demonstrations at scale, but the paper argues existing pipelines fall short in three specific ways. First, they lack automated quality control: "without an expert-level validation loop, many generated trajectories include execution failures or suboptimal grasps," which degrades downstream policy learning. Second, their domain randomization is "often superficial, yielding overly clean and homogeneous scenes that omit essential real-world factors such as clutter, lighting variation, and ambiguous language instructions." Third, they overlook cross-embodiment variation: "a low-degree-of-freedom (DoF) platform like the Piper often relies on lateral grasps due to its limited dexterity, whereas a high-DoF arm such as the Franka is capable of top-down precision grasps" for the same object — yet prior synthetic datasets rarely encode this embodiment-specific affordance structure.

RoboTwin 2.0 is explicitly a sequel. Its predecessor, RoboTwin 1.0 (Mu et al., CVPR 2025), "mirrored real demonstrations with simulated replicas for dual-arm benchmarking," and the paper's own comparison table places it against five other simulation platforms:

By the table's own bookkeeping, RoboTwin 2.0 is the only row with all three of domain randomization, automatic data generation, and VLA train/eval support checked at once — the pitch is to keep RoboTwin 1.0's automation and VLA-evaluation support while adding randomization and roughly 3.6x the task count (14 → 50).

// how it works

The method

RoboTwin 2.0 layers three mechanisms on top of a new asset library. The foundation is RoboTwin-OD, an object library of 731 annotated instances across 147 categories — including 153 objects across 27 categories folded in from Objaverse and 44 articulated instances across 9 categories from SAPIEN PartNet-Mobility, with the rest built and curated directly for RoboTwin-OD. Every object carries a grasp point, an object axis, and a functional point, plus up to 15 auto-generated natural-language descriptions that vary in shape, texture, functionality, part structure and granularity (the paper's own example for one shoe: "green shoe", "teal sneaker", "rubber sole running shoe", "blue and green running shoe", "half green half blue sneaker", "teal running shoe with thick beige sole").

On top of that asset library, an MLLM "code agent" automates expert-trajectory synthesis. Given a task's language description, an API list, and function examples, the agent emits a manipulation program, which is executed 10 times in simulation to average out stochastic variation in dynamics, control, and perception. A program is accepted once its measured success rate over those 10 runs exceeds 0.5; otherwise a VLM "observer" inspects the failed rollouts frame-by-frame, selects the specific failure mode from a structured execution log (unexecutable code, left-arm grasp failure, right-arm grasp failure, or incorrect target position), and feeds that diagnosis into a code-repair step — repeating until the program passes or a 5-iteration cap is hit.

The third component is embodiment-aware grasp adaptation. Because a low-DoF platform like Piper is often confined to lateral grasps while a high-DoF Franka can approach the same object top-down, RoboTwin-OD's per-object grasp annotations are expanded with angular perturbations "biased toward directions with higher arm reachability," and each of the five supported embodiments — Aloha-AgileX, ARX-X5, Piper, Franka, UR5 — draws its own candidate grasps from combining preferred operation directions, randomized pose perturbations, and parallelized motion-planning attempts.

Finally, every generated trajectory can be replayed under domain randomization along five axes: cluttered distractor objects, background textures (drawn from an 11,000-texture library built via generative AI plus human-in-the-loop filtering), lighting conditions, tabletop height (varied up to 3 cm, per the paper's appendix), and diverse language instructions (object descriptions are split 12-for-training/3-for-evaluation so evaluation-time language is genuinely held out). A separate 3D camera-pose jitter — random position and orientation perturbation, bounded to 1 cm displacement — is applied only in the real-robot transfer study discussed below; it is not one of the five core randomization axes used elsewhere in the paper.

accept program ⇔ SuccessRate(10 trials) > 0.5 // otherwise: VLM observer selects a failure mode from the execution log → code repair → retry, up to 5 iterations, then "Code Fail"
// what they found

The results

Code generation. On the subset of tasks common to both versions, average success rate (ASR) rises from 47.4% (RoboTwin 1.0 Vanilla, one-shot generation) to 63.9% (RoboTwin 1.0 + multimodal feedback, "MM FB"), and from 62.1% (RoboTwin 2.0 Vanilla) to 71.3% (RoboTwin 2.0 + MM FB). RoboTwin 2.0's architecture is cheaper even before feedback is added: its Vanilla setting reaches 62.1% ASR against RoboTwin 1.0 Vanilla's 47.4%, using less than half the code tokens (569.4 vs. 1236.6), and its fully-repaired setting converges in fewer refinement iterations than 1.0's (CR-Iter 1.76 vs. 2.42) while reaching a higher final ASR (71.3% vs. 63.9%).

Embodiment-aware grasp augmentation. Across 50 tasks x 5 embodiments, moving from RoboTwin 1.0 to RoboTwin 2.0's grasp augmentation raises average data-collection success rate from 52.2% to 60.5% (+8.3 points). The gain concentrates in low-DoF platforms:

MethodAloha-AgileXPiperFrankaUR5ARX-X5Average
RoboTwin 1.065.1%2.4%67.3%57.6%68.6%52.2%
RoboTwin 2.078.8%25.1%67.2%57.1%74.2%60.5%
Difference+13.7%+22.7%-0.1%-0.5%+5.6%+8.3%

Piper gains +22.7 points and Aloha-AgileX +13.7, while the two 7-DoF arms (Franka, UR5) are roughly flat — consistent with the paper's claim that extra grasp candidates mainly help robots whose "constrained planning spaces" otherwise block a task. (The paper's own prose describes the Aloha-AgileX gain as "13.5%," which doesn't match this table's own +13.7-point difference row — Piper's +22.7% and ARX-X5's +5.6% both match exactly, so this looks like a one-off internal slip rather than a wrong table.)

Policy robustness under domain shift. RDT and Pi0's released pretrained weights average 18.8% and 22.5% success respectively across the eight simulation tasks of Table 3 (five of which the paper selects specifically as "unseen tasks" for this fine-tuning study), all evaluated under domain-randomized conditions. Fine-tuning further on 9,600 trajectories from 32 tasks (300/task) collected without randomization ("+Clean") barely moves Pi0 (24.9%) and actually lowers RDT (14.6%). Collecting that same corpus with RoboTwin 2.0's randomization applied ("+Rand.") lifts both further — RDT to 24.8% (a paper-quoted +31.9% relative gain over the 18.8% baseline) and Pi0 to 29.1% (+29.3% relative) — which the paper reads as evidence for genuine robustness rather than a closing "Real-to-Sim gap," since the clean-data condition had equal access to simulation and still didn't help.

Sim-to-real transfer. On four physical bimanual tasks (Stack Bowls, Handover Block, Pick Bottle, Click Bell) run on the COBOT-Magic platform with RDT as the policy backbone, adding 1,000 domain-randomized synthetic trajectories to just 10 real demonstrations raises the success rate averaged across all four seen/unseen x cluttered/clean configurations by 24.4 points on average, with per-configuration gains of +13.5, +27.5, +23.5 and +33.0 points. A zero-shot policy trained solely on those 1,000 synthetic trajectories (no real data at all) still improves +21.0 and +20.5 points on the two unseen-background settings.

Configuration10 clean real+ 1k RoboTwin 2.01k RoboTwin 2.0 (0-shot)
Seen bg, not cluttered29.5%43.0% (+13.5)—
Seen bg, cluttered14.0%41.5% (+27.5)—
Unseen bg, not cluttered15.5%39.0% (+23.5)36.5% (+21.0)
Unseen bg, cluttered9.0%42.0% (+33.0)29.5% (+20.5)

The abstract headlines this as a "367% relative improvement" (few-shot) and a "228% relative gain" (zero-shot). Both trace to the single hardest row above — unseen background and cluttered, where the 10-demo baseline is just 9.0%: (42.0−9.0)/9.0 = 367% for the few-shot condition, and (29.5−9.0)/9.0 = 228% for zero-shot, with 42.0/9.0 ≈ 4.7x matching Figure 1's "4.7x" callout. The body text's own average across all four configurations — the +24.4-point absolute gain quoted above — is the more representative number.

Benchmark saturation. The full 50-task benchmark evaluates ACT, DP, DP3, RDT and Pi0 single-task fine-tuned from 50 clean demonstrations per task, tested with 100 rollouts under Easy (clean) and Hard (domain-randomized: clutter, lighting, textures, height variation) conditions on the Aloha-AgileX embodiment. Every policy drops sharply from Easy to Hard — RDT falls from 34.5% to 13.7% (−20.8 points) and Pi0 from 46.4% to 16.3% (−30.1 points), both figures the paper quotes directly — while the non-pretrained baselines nearly collapse (ACT 29.7%→1.7%, DP 28.0%→0.6%). DP3 has the best Easy-setting average (55.2%), but the paper itself flags that this result "partly stem[s] from perfect point clouds and clean background segmentation in simulation" — a simulation-only 3D-perception advantage, not necessarily one that would survive real point-cloud noise.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The paper's "strong domain randomization" is specifically scene-level: clutter, background texture, lighting, tabletop height (±3 cm), and language instructions. Section 5.3's own related-work discussion notes that prior domain-randomization literature also randomizes "mass, friction and control latency" for sim-to-real transfer — but nothing in RoboTwin 2.0's own method section (Section 2.2) randomizes dynamics parameters; the one physical perturbation applied anywhere is a 1 cm camera-pose jitter used only in the real-robot transfer study, not one of the five headline axes. That's a reasonable scope choice, but the paper's framing ("comprehensive domain randomization... along five axes") could be read as broader than what's actually varied.

The abstract's two most-quoted numbers — a 367% relative improvement (few-shot) and a 228% relative gain (zero-shot) — are not an average across the real-world study; they come from the single hardest of its four configurations in Table 4 (unseen background, cluttered scene), where the 10-demo baseline averages a small 9.0%, mechanically inflating any relative percentage. The body text's own more representative statistic — a 24.4-percentage-point average gain across all four configurations — never appears in the abstract. A third headline figure is stranger still: the abstract also claims "a 10.9% gain in code generation success rate," and that number appears exactly once in the entire paper — in that sentence. It is never derived, and Table 1's like-for-like pairings do not produce it (RoboTwin 2.0 beats 1.0 by 14.7 points comparing the two no-feedback rows and by 7.4 points comparing the two full-feedback rows; averaging across all three variant pairs gives 9.5). Whatever 10.9 measures, the paper does not show its working. Neither framing is false, but a reader who only sees the abstract (or Figure 1's "4.7x") would not know it is a worst-case cherry-pick rather than a typical result.

The paper's blanket claim that "models fine-tuned with clean data show negligible improvements in average success rate" (Section 4.3) doesn't hold uniformly: Pi0+Clean (24.9%) is indeed close to its 22.5% baseline, but RDT+Clean (14.6%) is actually below its 18.8% baseline — a regression, not a negligible improvement, for one of the paper's two policy backbones. The claim that "our system supports zero-shot generation of complex dual-arm behaviors beyond primitive pick-and-place actions," unlike "prior MLLM-based pipelines such as GenSim2 and RoboGen," is asserted once in the introduction; GenSim2 and RoboGen are never run as baselines anywhere in the results, so the comparison is not empirically demonstrated within this paper.

Table 5's real-per-rollout evaluation protocol is stated precisely (100 rollouts per task/policy/condition), but Table 4's real-robot experiment states no comparable trial count anywhere in the main text or the appendices covering policy training details — so the statistical weight behind deltas like a +33.0-point gain on a physical robot can't be assessed from what the paper reports.

baselines

ACT, DP, DP3, RDT and Pi0 span the standard imitation-learning-to-VLA range as of the paper's writing, but none of the VLA foundation models it name-checks in Related Work — OpenVLA, Octo, CogACT — are ever run on RoboTwin 2.0's own 50-task benchmark, so the Hard-setting collapse reported for ACT/DP/DP3 is not shown to generalize (or not) to today's stronger open VLA baselines.

contamination

Not the usual pretraining-corpus sense — the closer risk is sim-to-sim leakage: RDT and Pi0's own released pretraining data may already include RoboTwin-family or visually similar simulated bimanual scenes, which the paper doesn't audit, so their "released pretrained weights" numbers in Table 3 aren't guaranteed to be a clean zero-shot transfer test.

what's missed

The abstract's 367%/228% figures (and Figure 1's 4.7x) come from the single hardest, lowest-baseline row of Table 4, not the +24.4-point average the body text separately reports across all four real-world configurations.

would raise confidence

Stating the real-world rollout count per Table 4 cell (as Table 5 does for simulation: "100 rollouts"); running at least one current open VLA (OpenVLA/Octo/CogACT) through the Hard-setting benchmark; and auditing RDT/Pi0's pretraining data for prior exposure to RoboTwin-style simulated scenes.

// bottom line

RoboTwin 2.0 is a substantial, carefully-ablated engineering effort — 731 annotated objects, an MLLM-repair loop that measurably cuts code length and refinement iterations versus its own 1.0 baseline, and a five-axis scene randomization scheme that demonstrably helps both simulated robustness (Table 3) and real sim-to-real transfer (Table 4). But its two headline percentages are the least representative numbers in the paper, and its Hard-setting benchmark — while a real and current bottleneck for ACT, DP, DP3, RDT and Pi0 — has not yet been tested against the more capable open VLA baselines it cites as related work.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. RoboTwin 2.0 bundles three separable pieces — an MLLM-driven, simulation-in-the-loop code-repair pipeline (Figure 3); five scene-level domain-randomization axes (clutter, background, lighting, tabletop height, language); and per-embodiment grasp adaptation across five robots — into a 731-object, 50-task, five-embodiment package with 100,000+ pre-collected trajectories.
  2. Randomized synthetic pretraining, not just more synthetic data, is what buys robustness: pretraining RDT and Pi0 on domain-randomized synthetic trajectories gains +31.9%/+29.3% relative over their released-pretrained baselines (Table 3) — while pretraining on the same-size clean, non-randomized corpus barely moves Pi0 (22.5%→24.9%) and actually lowers RDT (18.8%→14.6%) — and real-robot transfer sees a 24.4-point average success-rate gain from just 10 real demos plus 1,000 synthetic trajectories (Table 4), though the abstract's headline "367%"/"228%" figures are the single hardest cell of that table, not the average.
  3. The Hard (domain-randomized) benchmark setting is still a real bottleneck: RDT and Pi0 drop 20.8 and 30.1 points from Easy to Hard, and non-pretrained ACT/DP collapse to 0.6–1.7%, on a benchmark that has not yet tested current open VLA baselines like OpenVLA, Octo, or CogACT.
